The reader knows what the friends do not

The book’s first verse gives a verdict before any trouble comes. Job is blameless and upright, fears God, and turns from evil. The LORD repeats those words in verse 8. Satan’s question in verse 9 sets the test: is such goodness only paid for? Job and his friends never hear this scene in heaven. The reader does. Every later claim that Job must have sinned is already known to be wrong.
Silence comes before the argument

Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar agree together to come and comfort Job (verse 11). They do not recognize him at first. They weep, tear their robes, and throw dust on their heads (verse 12). Verse 13 says they sat on the ground with him for seven days. No one spoke, because they saw how great his grief was. This silence is the best thing they do in the book. The trouble between them starts when they begin to explain.
Grief reverses the language of birth

Satan said Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). In verse 3 Job curses his birthday. He never curses God in this chapter. Verse 4 says, “Let that day be darkness.” That reverses the first words of creation in Genesis 1:3. His speech is made of “why” questions (verses 11, 12, 20). The text records his grief at full length and adds no rebuke.
Past counsel becomes a charge

Eliphaz opens with praise for Job’s past help to others (verses 3–4). Verse 5 turns that praise into a charge. Job could counsel sufferers, and now he cannot bear his own trouble. Verse 7 states the rule behind every speech the friends will make. The innocent do not perish. Eliphaz supports it from experience and from a vision (verses 8, 12–16). The reader knows from 1:1 that the rule does not fit this case.
Advice assumes an explanation

Much of what Eliphaz says here is fine teaching. Proverbs 3:11–12 says nearly the same as verse 17. The fault lies in where he applies it. He assumes Job’s pain is correction for a wrong. Chapter 1:8 has told the reader otherwise. His promises in verses 19–26 depend on Job accepting that account. Verse 27 closes the matter: we have searched it out, and it is so.
Failed friendship becomes a dry stream

Verse 14 says what Job wanted: kindness for a man who is failing. Verse 15 says what he got. He compares his friends to a desert stream. It runs full with melted ice in the cold season (verse 16). In the heat, when travelers need it, it is gone (verse 17). Caravans leave the road for it and die (verses 18–20). In verse 24 he asks them to name his error, which none has done.
Attention can feel like pursuit

From verse 7 on Job speaks to God, not about him. The friends never address God in the whole book. Psalm 8:4 asks, “What is man, that you think of him?” There the question is wonder at God’s care. Job asks nearly the same in verse 17 and means the opposite. God’s attention feels like being watched every moment (verse 18). In verse 19 he asks for time enough to swallow.
An argument makes the dead guilty

Bildad begins from a principle in verse 3: God does not pervert justice. Verse 4 applies it to ten dead children. He says “if,” but his meaning is plain. They died because they sinned. Chapter 1:5 showed Job offering sacrifices for them in case they had. Chapter 1:19 said a wind killed them. Bildad keeps his principle safe by making the dead guilty.
A court requires more than an argument

Job does not dispute God’s power; that power is his problem. The chapter is full of court language: answer, contend, judge (verses 3, 14–16, 32). A fair hearing needs two parties who can face each other. Verse 32 says God is not a man as Job is. Verse 33 names what is missing: an umpire over both. Job says no such person exists. The idea returns and grows in 16:19 and 19:25.
Creation becomes grounds for complaint

Verse 8 sets two acts of the same hands together: making and destroying. Verses 9–12 describe his forming with great tenderness. He was shaped like clay, clothed with skin, and given life and kindness. Psalm 139:13–15 uses such images for praise. Job uses them as grounds for complaint. A maker should not ruin his careful work (verse 3). The memory of care makes the present harder to understand.
Certainty closes the hearing

Zophar is the harshest of the three. Verse 6 says Job has received less than his guilt deserves. In verse 5 he claims to know what God would say. When God does speak in chapters 38–41, he says nothing of the kind. Chapter 42:7 says the friends did not speak rightly. Zophar himself declares that God’s depths cannot be searched (verses 7–9). That truth should have made him less certain.
Creation does not settle the dispute

The friends speak as if they hold a secret about God. In verses 7–9 Job says the birds and fish know it too. God’s hand is behind all that happens. That fact is common ground. What it means is the dispute. Verse 6 offers Job’s evidence: robbers live safely. Verses 13–25 list God’s power as overturning rulers, with no clear pattern of reward.
Defending God can involve false speech

Verse 4 calls the friends “forgers of lies.” Verses 7–8 explain the charge. They say untrue things about Job in order to defend God. Job asks whether God needs that kind of help. He predicts in verse 10 that God will rebuke them. Chapter 42:7 records that rebuke. Verse 5 says their silence would have been wisdom, as it was in 2:13.
A tree offers hope people lack

Verses 7–9 describe a stump that grows again when water reaches it. Verse 10 sets a human death against that picture. Job sees more hope for a tree than for himself. Then in verses 13–15 he imagines an exception. God might hide him, set a time, and remember him. He pictures God longing for the work of his hands. It is a wish, and verses 18–19 let it erode again.
A friend treats protest as danger

In chapters 4–5 Eliphaz was courteous. Here he opens with scorn (verses 2–3). Verse 4 makes a new charge. Job’s protest, he says, damages reverence and prayer for everyone. Verse 6 treats the protest itself as evidence of guilt. A man who complains this way must have something to hide. The portrait of the wicked in verses 20–35 is drawn to resemble Job’s losses.
A witness is needed beyond the friends

Verse 2 gives Job’s verdict on the friends. Verses 4–5 say what he would do in their place. He would use his mouth to strengthen and ease grief. He then describes God as an attacker (verses 9–14). Yet in verse 19 he says he has a witness in heaven. He appeals to God against what God has done to him. The friends have failed, so he looks for an advocate above them.
False brightness cannot remove death

The friends keep promising Job a bright future if he repents. Zophar said his darkness would become like morning (11:17). In verse 12 Job answers that promise. They call night day and say light is near while it is dark. He will not accept comfort that denies what he sees. Verses 13–16 state his honest expectation, which is the grave. A hope that ignores his condition is no help to him.
A general picture targets one sufferer

Verses 8–10 use six different words for traps and snares. Bildad says the wicked man walks into them by his own feet. The speech is framed as a general truth. Its details are not general. Disease consumes the skin (verse 13), and the tent is ruined (verse 15). Verse 19 says he has no child left. Each item matches what happened to Job.
An appeal interrupts accusation

Verses 13–19 list every bond Job has lost, from brothers to servants to wife. The three friends are all he has left. Verse 21 begs them twice for pity. Verse 22 says they pursue him as God does. Since they give none, he turns elsewhere. He wants a written record (verses 23–24) and a living Redeemer (verse 25). In Leviticus 25:25 a redeemer is a relative who steps in to help.
Zophar pictures wealth as swallowed food

Zophar builds his speech on pictures of eating (verses 12–23). Wickedness tastes sweet and then turns to venom. Verse 15 says God makes the man vomit up his wealth. The claim under the pictures is in verse 5. The success of the wicked is brief. Verse 19 adds a charge of crushing the poor, with no proof. This is Zophar’s last speech, and Job answers it with evidence in chapter 21.
Observation challenges the friends’ rule

The friends argue from a rule. Job argues in this chapter from what people can see. Verse 7 puts his question plainly. Verse 8 answers Bildad’s claim that the wicked leave no children (18:19). Verse 13 answers Zophar’s claim that their joy is short (20:5). In verse 19 he rejects the idea that the children pay later. Psalm 73:3–12 and Jeremiah 12:1 raise the same question.
Suspicion becomes an invented charge

Until now the friends have hinted at guilt. In verses 6–9 Eliphaz names crimes. He offers no witness and no instance. The charges are built to fit the theory that suffering proves sin. Chapter 1:8 gives God’s own opposite verdict. Job will answer each charge in 29:12–16 and 31:16–22. Verse 30 says a clean man’s prayer can rescue the guilty (see 42:8).
Absence prevents a hearing

Job wants a courtroom, and he is confident of a fair hearing (verses 6–7). His problem in verse 3 is that he cannot find the judge. Verses 8–9 search in four directions and find no one. Verse 10 turns the matter around. Job cannot see God, but God sees Job’s path. He expects the test to prove him gold. Verses 15–16 show that this trust and his fear exist together.
A complaint extends beyond one household

Job’s complaint now reaches past his own house. Verses 2–11 describe the poor in close detail. Workers carry grain while hungry and press grapes while thirsty (verses 10–11). Verse 12 gathers it up: the wounded cry out from the city. Job says God does not treat this as wrong. Eliphaz has just accused Job of crushing such people (22:6–9). This chapter shows whose side Job takes.
A short speech leaves the case unheard

The friends’ third round is running out of things to say. Bildad has six verses, and Zophar will not speak at all. Verse 4 repeats what Eliphaz said twice (4:17; 15:14). Job himself granted the point long ago (9:2). It does not touch his question about injustice in chapter 24. Verse 6 calls a human being a worm. In 1:8 God spoke of Job with pride.
Shared beliefs do not guarantee useful help

Verses 2–4 are sarcasm. Bildad’s speech was grand, and it helped no one. Job then praises God’s power better than Bildad did (verses 5–14). He shows that knowledge of God’s greatness is not what divides them. They all believe it. Verse 14 calls everything he has listed a whisper. Job claims to know less about God than his friends claim.
Job refuses a purchased agreement

The friends offer Job a way out: confess, and be restored. Verse 5 calls that a lie he will not tell. He swears by the same God he says has wronged him (verse 2). Verse 6 says he holds fast his righteousness. God used that very language about him in 2:3. His wife used it against him in 2:9. Verses 13–23 sound like the friends’ view, and readers explain that in different ways.
Mining skill exposes another limit

Verses 1–11 admire human skill. Miners reach places the falcon and the lion have never seen (verses 7–8). Verse 12 then asks the question that skill cannot answer. Wisdom is not in the deep, and no price buys it (verses 14–19). Verse 28 gives God’s word to humans. To fear the Lord is wisdom, and to turn from evil is understanding. Those are the words used of Job in 1:1.
Memory defines the lost public role

Verse 12 begins with “because.” Job’s honor at the gate had a cause. Verses 12–17 list it: the poor, the orphan, the dying, the widow. He was eyes, feet, and a father to people in need. Verse 16 says he looked into the cases of strangers. Eliphaz charged him with wronging these same groups (22:6–9). Job answers with his record, point by point.
The remembered world has been reversed

The word “now” opens three parts of this chapter (verses 1, 9, 16). Each sets the present against the honor of chapter 29. Verse 20 names the deepest loss. Job cries out, and God does not answer. He stands, and God only looks at him. Verse 25 recalls that he wept for others in their hard days. He gave what he does not receive.
A measure becomes an image of justice

Job asks for a fair weighing of his life in verse 6. An even balance is an honest scale. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. Verses 13–15 ground a servant’s rights in one Maker of both. His standard reaches inward, to the eyes and to gloating (verses 1 and 29). In verse 35 he signs and demands a reply. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.
Age does not settle authority

Verse 8 states Elihu’s claim to speak. Wisdom comes from the Almighty’s breath, so age does not decide it (verse 9). That is a fair point against the three older men. The chapter also says four times that he was angry (verses 2–5). Verses 18–20 describe a man bursting to talk. Neither Job nor God ever answers Elihu. Chapter 42:7 names the three friends and leaves him out.
An equal listener claims to explain God

Job wanted someone on his own level to hear him (9:32–33). In verse 6 Elihu offers himself as that equal. He adds an idea the three friends did not develop. Suffering may warn and teach; it is not only a penalty (verses 16–19). Verses 29–30 say God uses it to bring people back. That is a real advance in the debate. It still assumes Job needed correcting, which 1:8 denies.
A principle takes the place of a hearing

Verse 10 states a principle that the whole Bible affirms. God does not do wickedness. Elihu then uses it as a verdict on Job. If God is just, the man who complains must be wrong. Verse 11 repeats the friends’ rule that God repays each one’s work. Verses 7–8 accuse Job of walking with the wicked and cite nothing. A true principle takes the place of a hearing.
Unheard cries receive another explanation

Elihu grants in verse 9 that the oppressed cry out. Job said the same in 24:12. Elihu then explains why no answer comes. They cry from pain and do not truly seek God (verse 10). Verse 12 blames their pride. So an unanswered prayer becomes the fault of the one who prays. Job has already said his own prayer is pure (16:17).
Instruction and threat share one speech

Verse 15 sums up Elihu’s best thought. God rescues the afflicted by means of their affliction. Pain can open a person’s ear. Verses 11–12 then attach the old bargain: obey and prosper, refuse and perish. Job obeyed, and he did not prosper. So the teaching and a threat share one speech. In verses 27–33 Elihu turns to the storm, which prepares for chapter 38.
Weather prepares a change of voice

Verse 14 asks Job to stop and look at God’s works. Elihu’s questions in verses 15–18 sound like the ones God will ask. Verse 13 allows a storm more than one purpose. It may come for correction, for the land, or for kindness. That is wider than the friends’ single rule. A real storm seems to be gathering as he speaks. In 38:1 the LORD answers from the whirlwind.
Questions change the scale of the debate

Job asked for a hearing and thought none would come (23:3; 30:20). In verse 1 the LORD comes and speaks to him. The answer does not explain Job’s suffering. It never mentions the accuser or any charge. Verse 4 begins a long series of questions about the making of the world. Verses 26–27 describe rain falling where no person lives. The world is not arranged around human use or human reward.
Wild creatures live beyond human service

Every animal in this chapter lives outside human control. Verse 5 asks who set the wild donkey free. Verses 7–8 show it scorning the city and ranging the hills. The wild ox serves no farmer (verses 9–12). The ostrich lacks sense, and God made her so (verses 13–17). The friends described a tidy world. God shows one full of misfits.
Judgment includes the power to govern

Verse 8 names the real issue between them. To be in the right, Job has put God in the wrong. The friends did the reverse and put Job in the wrong. Both sides assumed that one of the two must be condemned. Verses 10–14 hand Job the task of governing. Let him bring down every proud person in the world. Running justice turns out to be harder than demanding it.
A creature resists the language of ownership

Verses 1–7 ask whether Job can hook, bind, bargain with, or sell this creature. Verse 8 warns him to try once and remember it. Verse 10 draws the point. If no one dares to rouse Leviathan, who can stand before its maker? Verse 11 adds that God owes nothing to anyone. That answers the accuser’s question about serving God for pay (1:9). It also answers the friends’ view of reward as wages.
The final judgment changes how the speeches should be read

Verse 7 changes how every speech in the book should be read. God says the friends did not speak rightly about him. He says his servant Job did, and repeats it in verse 8. Job protested, and the friends defended God. The honest protest is judged truer than the false defense. The friends now need the prayer of the man they accused. Verse 10 ties Job’s restoration to that prayer.
